I sit on three boards and I interview a lot of finance people, and there is one thing I listen for that almost nobody prepares. It is not what you decided. Outcomes are luck as often as they are judgement, and anyway I can read the outcome. What I want is what you knew at the moment you decided, and what you did not know. A candidate who says we chose option B and it worked has told me nothing at all. A candidate who says we had been running two systems for eighteen months, we had modelled three scenarios, and the one thing we did not have was any visibility on the renewal, has told me how they think. And the second half of that matters more than the first. Naming what you did not know is the single most senior thing anybody does in an interview, and it is very rare, because it feels like admitting you were not in control. You were not in control. Nobody is.

There are three parts to that, and I will take the middle one first because the other two depend on it. On governance, my recommendation would be that the audit committee review the reconciliation policy before the year end, not after it, on the grounds that the same exception has now appeared twice. On the systems question, it is not imperative that we decide this quarter, and I would caution against deciding before we have the migration cost. And on the third, which was whether I would keep the current controller structure, my answer is no, and I would put forward a single shared function instead. I should say that the second of those three is the one I am least certain about, and if the board wanted to defer it by a quarter I would not argue.

Margaret asks Fernando to describe a decision rather than a result. Fernando sets out what had already happened before the meeting. Fernando names the trade-off that decided it. Margaret asks what he did not know at that moment. Fernando names the one thing he could not see and says the outcome flattered the decision.
